entities.summary:
Dubai, the most populous city in the United Arab Emirates (UAE), emerged as a significant urban center around June 9, 1833, when a group of 800 members of the Bani Yas tribe, led by Sheikh Maktoum bin Butti, settled in the area. Strategically located on the southern shore of the Persian Gulf, Dubai has evolved from a modest fishing village into a global city and a major business hub, reflecting broader trends in economic globalization and urbanization in the Modern Era. It matters in world history as a symbol of rapid development and modernization in the Arab world, showcasing how traditional societies can adapt and thrive in the contemporary global economy.

The transformation of Dubai was catalyzed by its discovery of oil in the 1960s, which fueled unprecedented economic growth, attracting expatriates and investors from around the globe. The establishment of the Dubai International Airport in 1960 and subsequent expansion positioned the city as a critical aviation hub, connecting East and West. Landmark developments such as the Burj Khalifa, completed in 2010, and the Palm Jumeirah, a remarkable feat of engineering, epitomize Dubai's ambition to reshape its identity and leverage tourism and commerce as key economic drivers.

Dubai's legacy is reflected in its role as a model for urban development in the 21st century, influencing cities worldwide to adopt similar growth strategies. As a result of its dynamic economy, the city has attracted a diverse population, with more than 200 nationalities coexisting, which has transformed its cultural landscape. Furthermore, Dubai's approach to sustainable development and innovation in architecture has inspired other cities facing similar challenges of growth and environmental sustainability, positioning it as a leading case study in global urbanization.
